title: Summer Avot
hook: a chapter of Pirkei Avot each summer Shabbat afternoon
tomorrow: why would anyone skip haircuts for three weeks?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shavuot night: the people slept in at Sinai, so some stay up learning. Awake for the gift. After Shavuot the summer opens, and so does a small book.

Long summer afternoons have a way of dissolving: a nap, a screen, and suddenly the light is gone. Some Jews give one of those hours, on Shabbat, to a short book of sayings: Pirkei Avot, a chapter a week. Open a siddur to it and something looks odd. Before each chapter sits a line that isn't from Avot. After it, another line from somewhere else entirely. Why would every chapter start with a borrowed line?
screen: `A LONG SUMMER AFTERNOON.` → `A CHAPTER A WEEK.` → `A BORROWED LINE BEFORE AND AFTER.`

segments.voice: The line before comes from another part of the Mishnah, tractate Sanhedrin: all Israel have a share in the world to come. The line after comes from tractate Makkot: Rabbi Chananya ben Akashya says the Holy One wanted to give Israel merit, and so gave them much Torah and many commandments. So every chapter of hard, practical advice sits between two promises: you belong, and all of this is a gift. That's the puzzle solved. And the sayings inside can sting. Avot opens with a chain, Moses received Torah at Sinai and handed it on, to say these short lines are Torah too, passed hand to hand. Then: be deliberate in judgment. Hillel: if I am not for myself, who will be for me? Rabbi Tarfon: it is not your duty to finish the work, but neither are you free to stop. Read cold, that's a lot of pressure for a lazy afternoon. Read inside the frame, it changes: you already have a place, and the work is handed to you, not dumped on you. The custom is a chapter each Shabbat afternoon through the summer months, and some go around the cycle more than once. One chapter takes a few minutes. Slow enough to remember one saying by Sunday.
screen: `BEFORE: A SHARE FOR ALL ISRAEL.` · `AFTER: MUCH TORAH, AS A GIFT.` · `A CHAIN FROM SINAI.` · `NOT YOURS TO FINISH.` · then, large: `SUMMER SAYINGS.`

segments.voice: Choose one saying from today, maybe Rabbi Tarfon's: not yours to finish, not free to stop. Stand, if you can, and walk slowly for about a minute, saying it silently in time with your steps. When you sit back down, notice which half of the line stayed with you.
screen: `ONE SAYING.` · `A SLOW MINUTE'S WALK.` · `WHICH HALF STAYED?`

segments.voice: Summer Avot: a chapter of Pirkei Avot each summer Shabbat afternoon, every chapter held between two borrowed promises.
Here's the line: summer sayings, one chapter, one afternoon, one saying to keep. Back tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Jewish communities read a chapter of Pirkei Avot on Shabbat afternoons in the summer, each chapter introduced by Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1 and closed with the saying of Rabbi Chananya ben Akashya.

fork.setup: summer job, your little sister, your grandpa's garden: too much to do, and Sunday is already here. which Avot saying fits?
options: Rabbi Tarfon: not yours to finish, not free to stop.
be deliberate in judgment: decide nothing until you're sure.
if I am not for myself: drop the rest and rest.
fork.reveal: Tarfon's line is made for this: do your part of the work without carrying the whole of it. Hillel's line goes on: if I am only for myself, what am I?

original.note: Hebrew: fathers; Pirkei Avot, the Chapters of the Fathers.

what a scholar hears: Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1 is read before each chapter, and Makkot 3:16 (Rabbi Chananya ben Akashya, citing Isaiah 42:21) after.

chat.says: Owen's grandma came home on hospice. he asked if judaism has anything for 'when you can't fix it'
options: Rabbi Tarfon: it's not on you to finish the work, but you can keep showing up.
Avot says if you work hard enough, you can fix almost anything.
Judaism says don't get involved with what you can't change at all.
chat.meaning: Avot's sayings come framed as a gift. Rabbi Tarfon: you don't have to finish the work, and you're not free to stop.

Pirkei Avot.meaning: Chapters of the Fathers: the Mishnah's book of sayings

Rabbi Tarfon.meaning: a sage of the Mishnah: not yours to finish the work

Rabbi Chananya ben Akashya.meaning: the sage whose saying closes each chapter in the siddur

sources.ref: Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1 (all Israel have a share in the world to come), read before each chapter
Mishnah Makkot 3:16 (Rabbi Chananya ben Akashya, citing Isaiah 42:21), read after each chapter
Pirkei Avot 1:1, 1:14, 2:16 (the chain from Sinai; be deliberate in judgment; Hillel; Rabbi Tarfon)

notes: Puzzle shape: the strange detail is the borrowed frame around each chapter (Sanhedrin 10:1 before, Makkot 3:16 after), as printed in the siddur. Confirm it is described as a custom of reading, not part of Avot itself.
Season kept general ('through the summer months'); customs differ on start and end (from Passover, to Shavuot or to Rosh Hashanah) and on repeating the cycle. Confirm.
